premises.text: Open-source and free software is ubiquitous but full of bugs and missing features, and support is hard because users lack time/skill to patch while developers dislike unpaid bug work—a knowledge/priority mismatch
premises.evidence_span: all this software has two properties in common, which is bugs and missing features

premises.text: Integrations on major issue trackers let users place paid incentives on issues in two clicks (multi-user crowdfunding) and let developers request incentives or list for crowdfunding in one click
premises.evidence_span: allows you to pay or get paid directly from an issue page

premises.text: Company takes 6% on successful incentives and shares a fee with issue-system hosters, turning trackers into profit centers
premises.evidence_span: we take a 6% fee for each successful incentive

premises.text: Same incentive panel can expand beyond open source to Apple and Google app stores
premises.evidence_span: Our next focus would be the Apple and Google app stores

value.text: Users get the support or improvements they need and developers get paid for fixing issues
value.evidence_span: get the support you really need or where it's easy to get something improved

secondary_value.text: Add monetization to the open-source market
secondary_value.evidence_span: adding a monetization element to the entire open source market

causal_links.evidence_span: mismatch in knowledge and priority between the user and the developer
pay or get paid directly from an issue page
turns an issue system into a profit center
not at all limited to open source

notes: OS ubiquity examples folded as framing; bugs/missing features + hard support + developer mismatch as one problem (§4.1.6). Tracker integrations, user incentive flow, and developer ask/list folded as one issue-page mechanism (§4.1.7). Market-size ambition framing excluded. ASR 'book' for bug left in spans where present. Four-domain partition; not a need/product/money triad.
